instruction: Explain the core anatomical structure and physiological mechanisms of the Master Deconstructed Assembly (26-Part Knolling Kit).
input:
Source Material: STOIC MASTER ANATOMICAL MATRIX & MECHANICAL ASSEMBLY:
1. Cutaneous & Muscular Actuators: Pectoralis major (Class 3 lever, adduction/internal rotation), Rectus abdominis (flexion of vertebral column, hydrostatic abdominal press), Deltoid (scapular fulcrum).
2. Skeletal Framework: Calvarium (rigid protective shell), Sternum (anterior strut), Rib cage (compliant thoracic basket), Vertebral column (axial compression dampener), Pelvic girdle (mechanical load transmitter to femurs).
3. Visceral Core: Left Ventricle (high-pressure systemic pump, 120 mmHg systolic), Right Ventricle (pulmonary bellows, 25 mmHg), Lungs (gas-liquid interface, dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine surfactant preventing atelectasis), Liver (dual portal-systemic metabolic factory), Kidneys (countercurrent multiplier, NKCC2 cotransporter in thick ascending limb).
4. Neurovascular Conduits: Ascending Aorta (Windkessel elastic buffering), Inferior Vena Cava (capacitance return), Cerebrum & Brainstem (cranial nerve origins, cardiac & vasomotor control centers).
output:
Under strict STOIC clinical grounding, the Master Deconstructed Assembly (26-Part Knolling Kit) operates as follows:

STOIC MASTER ANATOMICAL MATRIX & MECHANICAL ASSEMBLY:
1. Cutaneous & Muscular Actuators: Pectoralis major (Class 3 lever, adduction/internal rotation), Rectus abdominis (flexion of vertebral column, hydrostatic abdominal press), Deltoid (scapular fulcrum).
2. Skeletal Framework: Calvarium (rigid protective shell), Sternum (anterior strut), Rib cage (compliant thoracic basket), Vertebral column (axial compression dampener), Pelvic girdle (mechanical load transmitter to femurs).
3. Visceral Core: Left Ventricle (high-pressure systemic pump, 120 mmHg systolic), Right Ventricle (pulmonary bellows, 25 mmHg), Lungs (gas-liquid interface, dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine surfactant preventing atelectasis), Liver (dual portal-systemic metabolic factory), Kidneys (countercurrent multiplier, NKCC2 cotransporter in thick ascending limb).
4. Neurovascular Conduits: Ascending Aorta (Windkessel elastic buffering), Inferior Vena Cava (capacitance return), Cerebrum & Brainstem (cranial nerve origins, cardiac & vasomotor control centers).

Clinical Pearls:
- Pectoralis major clavicular head is innervated by lateral pectoral nerve; sternocostal head by medial and lateral pectoral nerves.
- Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant composed predominantly of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine; deficiency leads to ARDS/NRDS.
- Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle expresses NKCC2 cotransporter, selectively blocked by loop diuretics like furosemide.

instruction: Explain the core anatomical structure and physiological mechanisms of the Cardiovascular & Hemodynamic System.
input:
Source Material: STOIC CARDIOVASCULAR PHYSIOLOGY & PATHOLOGY:
1. Left Ventricular Biomechanics: The left ventricle is 3x thicker than the right ventricle to overcome systemic vascular resistance (SVR ~ 120 mmHg vs 25 mmHg). Coronary artery perfusion to the left ventricle occurs predominantly during DIASTOLE because high intramyocardial systolic pressure compresses subendocardial vessels.
2. Windkessel Effect: The ascending aorta contains high elastin fiber content, expanding during systole and passively recoiling during diastole to drive forward organ perfusion.
3. Valve Hemodynamics: Aortic stenosis produces a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, associated with pulsus parvus et tardus (weak, delayed carotid pulses).
output:
Under strict STOIC clinical grounding, the Cardiovascular & Hemodynamic System operates as follows:

STOIC CARDIOVASCULAR PHYSIOLOGY & PATHOLOGY:
1. Left Ventricular Biomechanics: The left ventricle is 3x thicker than the right ventricle to overcome systemic vascular resistance (SVR ~ 120 mmHg vs 25 mmHg). Coronary artery perfusion to the left ventricle occurs predominantly during DIASTOLE because high intramyocardial systolic pressure compresses subendocardial vessels.
2. Windkessel Effect: The ascending aorta contains high elastin fiber content, expanding during systole and passively recoiling during diastole to drive forward organ perfusion.
3. Valve Hemodynamics: Aortic stenosis produces a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, associated with pulsus parvus et tardus (weak, delayed carotid pulses).

Clinical Pearls:
- Left coronary artery blood flow occurs primarily during diastole due to intramyocardial systolic compression.
- Aortic dissection Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta and requires urgent open surgical repair.
- Subendocardial infarction is most vulnerable during tachycardia because diastole duration is selectively shortened.

instruction: Explain the core anatomical structure and physiological mechanisms of the Respiratory & Alveolar Exchange.
input:
Source Material: STOIC RESPIRATORY SYSTEM & VENTILATORY MECHANICS:
1. Gas-Liquid Surface Tension: According to the Law of Laplace (P = 2T / r), smaller alveoli have higher collapsing pressures. Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine), which reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents end-expiratory atelectasis.
2. Gas Diffusion: Fick's Law of diffusion dictates that transfer rate is proportional to surface area and partial pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis increases membrane thickness, causing diffusion limitation and exertional dyspnea.
3. Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q): V/Q is highest at the apex (~3.0) and lowest at the base (~0.6) of the upright lung due to gravity-dependent blood flow distribution.

STOIC RESPIRATORY SYSTEM & VENTILATORY MECHANICS:
1. Gas-Liquid Surface Tension: According to the Law of Laplace (P = 2T / r), smaller alveoli have higher collapsing pressures. Type II pneumocytes secrete pulmonary surfactant (dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine), which reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents end-expiratory atelectasis.
2. Gas Diffusion: Fick's Law of diffusion dictates that transfer rate is proportional to surface area and partial pressure gradient, and inversely proportional to membrane thickness. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis increases membrane thickness, causing diffusion limitation and exertional dyspnea.
3. Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q): V/Q is highest at the apex (~3.0) and lowest at the base (~0.6) of the upright lung due to gravity-dependent blood flow distribution.

Clinical Pearls:
- Inhaled foreign objects most frequently lodge in the right mainstem bronchus because it is wider, shorter, and more vertically oriented than the left.
- Lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio (L/S ratio) > 2.0 in amniotic fluid indicates fetal lung maturity.
- Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction shunts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli to optimize V/Q matching.

instruction: Explain the core anatomical structure and physiological mechanisms of the Neuroanatomy & Central Processing.
input:
Source Material: STOIC NEUROANATOMY & CLINICAL LOCALIZATION:
1. Motor Pathways: The corticospinal tract arises from Betz pyramidal cells in precentral motor cortex (Brodmann area 4), descends through the posterior limb of internal capsule, and decussates at the cervicomedullary junction (medullary pyramids) before synapsing on anterior horn motor neurons.
2. Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron: UMN lesions cause hyperreflexia, spasticity (clasp-knife), and positive Babinski sign. LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, muscle fasciculations, severe atrophy, and hyporeflexia.
3. Cranial Nerve Course: Cranial nerve IV (trochlear) is unique: it is the ONLY cranial nerve to exit the brainstem dorsally, and it completely decussates before exiting. Palsy causes vertical diplopia that worsens when looking down and inward.
output:
Under strict STOIC clinical grounding, the Neuroanatomy & Central Processing operates as follows:

STOIC NEUROANATOMY & CLINICAL LOCALIZATION:
1. Motor Pathways: The corticospinal tract arises from Betz pyramidal cells in precentral motor cortex (Brodmann area 4), descends through the posterior limb of internal capsule, and decussates at the cervicomedullary junction (medullary pyramids) before synapsing on anterior horn motor neurons.
2. Upper vs Lower Motor Neuron: UMN lesions cause hyperreflexia, spasticity (clasp-knife), and positive Babinski sign. LMN lesions cause flaccid paralysis, muscle fasciculations, severe atrophy, and hyporeflexia.
3. Cranial Nerve Course: Cranial nerve IV (trochlear) is unique: it is the ONLY cranial nerve to exit the brainstem dorsally, and it completely decussates before exiting. Palsy causes vertical diplopia that worsens when looking down and inward.

Clinical Pearls:
- Trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the only nerve that exits the brainstem from the dorsal surface.
- Broca's aphasia involves inferior frontal gyrus (motor non-fluent speech with intact comprehension).
- Wernicke's aphasia involves superior temporal gyrus (fluent receptive speech with impaired comprehension).
